paras.text: Construction Liens, Insurance, and Bonds, Audio Lecture
This is the heaviest category on the business and law half. Eleven of your fifty questions come from this one chapter. Nothing else comes close.

It is also the chapter people try to memorize as a pile of loose numbers, and that is why it does not stick. So we are going to do it differently. Almost all of this chapter is one story, the story of a job where somebody does not get paid, told in the order it actually happens. Once the story is in your head the deadlines have somewhere to live.
Then we will do insurance, which is one skill, given a loss, name the policy. And bonds, which is one idea, a bond protects somebody other than you.
Idea one. What a lien actually is, and the ceiling on it.

Michigan's Construction Lien Act is M C L five seventy point eleven oh one and following. It is Act four ninety seven of nineteen eighty. It gives contractors, subcontractors, suppliers, and laborers a legal claim against the real property they improved when they do not get paid. Not against the owner personally. Against the house.
Two ceilings sit on top of that claim, and the second one is the whole philosophy of the act.
First ceiling. Your own lien can never exceed your contract price minus what you have already been paid. Obvious enough.

Second ceiling. The total of everyone's liens against the owner can never exceed what the owner agreed to pay the general contractor, minus the payments the owner properly made through sworn statements and lien waivers.

That second one is called the no double payment principle, and it explains almost every piece of paper in this chapter. An owner who pays correctly, with the right paperwork in hand, cannot be made to pay twice for the same work. Every form we are about to walk through exists either to protect the owner from paying twice, or to protect you from not getting paid once.
Now the story. A job starts, and the paperwork happens in this order.
Idea two. The notice of commencement, and the residential versus commercial split.

On a residential project the owner prepares the notice of commencement, but only when somebody asks for it. A contractor, sub, supplier, or laborer sends a written request by certified mail, and the owner then has ten days from the postmark to complete the form and return it. If the owner blows those ten days, the owner can end up paying the expenses the requester runs up digging out the information themselves. If the owner does not live at the site, a copy has to be posted conspicuously at the site.

Here is the trap, and it is one of the most reliable ones in the chapter. The residential notice of commencement is not recorded anywhere. It is provided on request, and posted. Commercial is the opposite. A commercial owner records the notice of commencement with the register of deeds before physical work begins.

Residential, on request and posted. Commercial, recorded before work starts. One more residential detail worth a point, the form must have a blank notice of furnishing attached to it, easily detachable, so the people downstream can use it.
Question. On a residential job, who prepares the notice of commencement, when, and where does it get recorded. Say it out loud.

The owner prepares it, only after a written request by certified mail, within ten days of the postmark, and it is not recorded at all. If the answer choice has a homeowner recording anything with the register of deeds, that is the commercial rule wearing a residential hat.
Idea three. The notice of furnishing, which is how invisible people become visible.

Think about the owner's problem. The owner hired you. The owner has never met your drywall sub or the lumberyard. The notice of furnishing is how those people raise a hand and say, we are here, we expect to get paid.

A subcontractor or supplier must serve it within twenty days after first furnishing labor or material. Twenty days from the first day on the job, not the last. That direction catches people, because every other lien deadline in this chapter runs from the last day.

It gets served on the designee named in the notice of commencement and on the general contractor, personally or by certified mail, and certified mail service is complete the moment it is mailed, not when it is received. If no designee is named, you serve the owner.
Who does not file one. The general contractor. Anyone in a direct contract with the owner is exempt, for the obvious reason that the owner already knows they exist.

Laborers have their own clock. A laborer's notice for unpaid wages is thirty days, and watch the trigger, it runs thirty days after the wages were due and not paid, not thirty days after starting work. For unpaid fringe benefits or withholdings, the deadline is the fifth day of the second month after the month they went unpaid.

Now a subtle one the exam does test. What happens if a sub serves the notice late. A late notice does not kill the lien. Everything furnished after the late notice is fully protected. Everything furnished before it is also protected, except to the extent the owner already paid the general contractor for that work while relying on a sworn statement or a lien waiver. So a late notice costs you only the money that already properly went out the door. The exception is the laborer. A laborer who misses the wage notice deadline loses the lien for those wages entirely.
Question. Your tile sub started March first. What is the deadline for the notice of furnishing, and what does the sub lose by filing it two months late.

Twenty days after first furnishing, so twenty days from March first. Filing late does not destroy the lien, it only gives up the amounts the owner already properly paid the general contractor against a sworn statement or waiver.
Idea four. The sworn statement, which is the owner's shield.
A sworn statement is a notarized list of every sub and supplier you contracted with, plus any unpaid laborers, showing each one's contract price, the amount paid, and the amount still owing.

You must give one to the owner whenever payment is due, whenever you ask for payment, or whenever the owner demands it. A subcontractor gives one to the general contractor on those same payment triggers, and to the owner on demand.

Here is why it matters so much. The owner is allowed to rely on it. Relying on your sworn statement, the owner can withhold what is owed to the subs, or pay those subs directly. That is the mechanism that makes the no double payment principle work in practice.

Which is exactly why the penalty is severe. Giving a false sworn statement with intent to defraud is a crime, on top of civil fraud liability. And if you ever sue to foreclose a lien, your complaint has to show that you provided a sworn statement if one was requested or required.
Idea five. The claim of lien, and the ninety day wall.

You record the claim of lien within ninety days after your last furnishing of labor or material, with the register of deeds for the county where the property sits. Not with a court. The register of deeds.
Three things about those ninety days.

They run from your own last day of real contract work. Warranty visits, courtesy callbacks, and punch list touch ups do not restart the clock. Do not let a friendly return trip fool you into thinking you bought more time.
The deadline is absolute. No extensions, no good cause exception. This is one of the few places in Michigan law with no mercy in it at all.
And a sub or supplier has to attach proof that the notice of furnishing was served.

Then one more short clock. Within fifteen days after recording, you serve a copy of the recorded claim of lien on the designee, or on the owner if there is no designee, personally or by certified mail.
Question. Two numbers. How long to record the claim of lien, and how long after recording to serve it.
Ninety days from last furnishing to record. Fifteen days from recording to serve.
Idea six. Turning a lien into money.
A recorded lien is not money. It is leverage. It clouds the title, so the house cannot be cleanly sold or refinanced. But leverage expires.
To turn it into money you file a foreclosure action, and you have exactly one year from the date the claim of lien was recorded. Miss the year and the lien simply expires, quietly, on its own.

The suit goes in circuit court for the county where the property is located. It is an equitable action, and when you file it you record a notice of lis pendens with the register of deeds, which is a public flag that litigation is pending on that property.
And there is a sweetener. The court may award reasonable attorney fees to a prevailing lien claimant. That cuts both ways, it can also award fees against you if your suit was vexatious.
So the full chain, and you should be able to say it in one breath. Twenty days to announce yourself, ninety days to record, fifteen days to serve, one year to sue.
Idea seven. The residential overlay, which is where builders get wiped out.
Michigan bolted an extra layer onto the lien act to protect homeowners, and it is brutal if you ignore it.

On a residential structure, a contractor has no lien at all unless the work was done under a written contract with the owner, and any amendments or change orders are in writing too. That written contract has to contain the statutory statement about licensing, and if a license is required for the work, your license number.
There is no dollar threshold on this. None. A handshake deal on a thirty five thousand dollar remodel means no lien. Not a reduced lien, no lien.

And if an unlicensed person records a lien on residential property anyway, the owner can sue to discharge it, and the unlicensed filer is liable for all the resulting damages, including actual costs and attorney fees. So the bad paperwork does not just cost you the lien, it can cost you money going the other direction.

The case that settled this is Stokes versus Millen Roofing. An unlicensed residential contractor cannot enforce the contract, cannot recover the value of the work under quantum meruit, which is the fallback claim for the fair value of work done, and has no lien. Nothing. If you sue on work that requires a license, you must plead and prove you were licensed.
Question. Verbal agreement, forty thousand dollar kitchen, you are fully licensed, work is perfect, homeowner refuses to pay. Do you have a lien.
No. Residential liens require a written contract with the licensing statement and your license number, at any dollar amount. Being licensed is necessary but it is not sufficient. Get it in writing.
Idea eight. The four lien waivers.
Michigan recognizes exactly four statutory waivers, and the exam will make you tell them apart. It is a simple grid, two questions.
Question one, how much does it release. A full waiver releases all lien rights. A partial waiver releases only a stated amount.
Question two, when does it take effect. An unconditional waiver is effective the moment it is signed. A conditional waiver is effective only upon actual payment of the amount shown.
Full or partial, conditional or unconditional. Four boxes.

The practical rule falls right out of it. Sign conditional waivers before the check clears. Sign unconditional only after the money is actually yours. An unconditional waiver handed over against a promise is a signature giving up your rights for nothing.
Three more waiver rules that get tested.

Advance waivers are void. Nobody can require you, as part of the contract, to waive your lien rights before the work is performed. That clause is against public policy and invalid, so a contract that contains one does not strip your rights.
Accepting a promissory note does not by itself waive your lien. Taking an I O U is not the same as giving up the claim.

And on residential jobs, if a homeowner receives a waiver from somebody other than the claimant who signed it, say the general hands over a stack of sub waivers, the homeowner cannot rely on it without verifying with the actual claimant that it is authentic, in writing, by phone, or in person.
The forms themselves carry the practical warning, do not sign blank or incomplete waiver forms, and keep a copy of everything you sign.
Question. You are handed a check on Friday for a progress payment. Which waiver do you sign, and when.

Conditional and partial. Conditional because it only takes effect when the payment actually happens, partial because it releases only that stated amount. Unconditional after the funds clear, if at all.
Now a trap that is pure memory, so I am just going to hand it to you.

The Homeowner Construction Lien Recovery Fund is gone. Abolished. Repealed by Public Act one forty seven of twenty ten, effective August twenty third, twenty ten. Builders used to pay into it, and homeowners and subs could recover out of it. It does not exist.

If an answer choice describes the recovery fund as a current remedy, or as a current license fee, it is wrong. The only true present tense statement about that fund is that it was abolished in twenty ten.
Now we switch subjects. Insurance.
There is really only one skill being tested here. Given a loss, name the policy. Three policies, three lanes, and they do not overlap.

Builders risk is first party property insurance, which means it pays you for damage to your own thing. It covers the structure while it is under construction, plus materials on site, in transit, or in storage, against perils like fire, wind, and theft. Half built house burns down, that is builders risk. Lumber package stolen off the slab, builders risk. Either the owner or the contractor can buy it, the contract should say which, and it ends at completion.

What it does not do. It does not cover injuries. It does not cover other people's property. And it does not cover your tools. Tools and equipment ride on an inland marine policy, sometimes called an equipment floater. If a question is about a stolen compressor or a saw that walked off, the answer is inland marine, not builders risk.

Commercial general liability, C G L, is third party coverage. Other people. Bodily injury and property damage to other people, arising out of your operations or your completed operations. A visitor trips over your ladder. Your crew cracks the neighbor's windshield. A connection you soldered lets go a year later and floods the finished kitchen. All C G L.

And here is the exclusion that matters more than anything else in your real business. C G L never pays to redo your own defective work. It is called the your work exclusion. General liability is not a warranty on your craftsmanship. It pays for the damage your bad work did to other things, not for going back and doing your work again.

Workers compensation covers your employees, on a no fault basis, and it is generally the employee's exclusive remedy against you. That phrase means the hurt employee takes the comp benefits instead of suing you.

Michigan's thresholds have two prongs and the exam wants both. Coverage is required if you regularly employ three or more employees at one time. Or, and this is the prong people forget, if you employ fewer than three but at least one employee has worked thirty five or more hours per week for thirteen or more weeks during the preceding fifty two weeks. So one steady full time helper triggers mandatory coverage all by himself. Public employers are always covered.

Then the rule that should change how you run your subs, the statutory principal rule. If a general contractor hires a sub that carries no comp insurance, and that sub's worker gets hurt, the general contractor pays the comp benefits as if it had employed that worker directly. That is M C L four eighteen point one seventy one.

That single rule is why you collect a certificate of insurance from every sub before they set foot on the site, and why you watch the expiration dates on those certificates. An additional insured endorsement goes one step further, extending the sub's liability policy to protect you as well.
Question. Your framing crew drops a bundle of sheathing through the neighbor's garage roof, and one of your guys breaks his wrist doing it. Which policies answer, one for each.

The neighbor's garage is C G L, other people's property. The broken wrist is workers compensation, your employee. And if the answer choice offers builders risk for either of those, it is wrong, builders risk is for the structure you are building.
Last topic. Bonds.
Start with the one sentence that carries most of the bond questions. A bond is not insurance for the contractor. It protects somebody else.

A surety bond has three parties. The principal, that is you, the contractor whose performance is being guaranteed. The obligee, the party the bond protects, an owner or a government unit. And the surety, the company standing behind the promise.

The surety expects to lose nothing. If the surety pays out on a claim, you have to pay the surety back. Insurance spreads your risk. A bond guarantees your promise to somebody else, with you still on the hook.
Four types to know.

A license or permit bond guarantees you will comply with a law or ordinance. Think municipal permit bonds for right of way or sidewalk work. And note this, the state residential builder license itself does not require a bond.
A bid bond guarantees that if you win the job, you will actually sign the contract and post the required bonds.
A performance bond guarantees the job gets completed per the plans and specs. On public work it protects the governmental unit, solely.
A payment bond guarantees that the subs, suppliers, and laborers get paid, and it protects only those claimants.

Michigan public work has hard numbers. On any public contract exceeding fifty thousand dollars, the contractor must furnish both a performance bond and a payment bond before the contract is awarded. Each bond is set by the governmental unit but cannot be less than twenty five percent of the contract amount.

Now, why does the payment bond exist at all. Because you cannot record a construction lien against public property. No lien on the courthouse. No lien on the school. The entire lien machinery we just spent twenty minutes on does not apply. So the unpaid sub on public work has one remedy, a claim on the payment bond, and the bond is standing in for the lien.

That claim has its own clock. A claimant with no direct contract with the principal contractor must serve written notice on the principal contractor within thirty days after first furnishing. And must give written notice of the claim to both the principal contractor and the governmental unit within ninety days after last furnishing. All by certified mail. Suit on the bond is allowed once you have gone unpaid for ninety days after your last furnishing.
Question. Who does a performance bond protect, and could you lien a public school if you went unpaid.
The performance bond protects the obligee, on public work the governmental unit, never you. And no, you can never lien public property. The payment bond is the substitute.
Time for the rapid fire recap. Say these out loud with me. If one of them is a blank, that is tonight's drilling.

Construction Lien Act, M C L five seventy point eleven oh one and following. Residential notice of commencement, returned within ten days of the request, posted if the owner lives elsewhere, never recorded. Commercial notice of commencement, recorded before work begins. Notice of furnishing for subs and suppliers, twenty days from first furnishing, served on the designee and the general contractor. Laborer wage notice, thirty days from wages due but unpaid. Claim of lien, recorded with the register of deeds within ninety days of last furnishing, absolute deadline, warranty work does not count. Serve the recorded lien within fifteen days. Foreclosure, circuit court, within one year of recording, with a lis pendens, attorney fees possible for the prevailing claimant. Residential lien requires a written contract with the license number, at any dollar amount. Four waivers, full and partial, conditional and unconditional. Conditional means effective only on actual payment. Advance waivers void. Recovery fund abolished, twenty ten. Workers comp, three employees at one time, or one employee at thirty five hours for thirteen weeks. Uninsured sub, the general pays under M C L four eighteen point one seventy one. Builders risk covers the building, C G L covers other people, comp covers your crew, inland marine covers your tools. Public work over fifty thousand dollars, performance bond and payment bond, each at least twenty five percent. Performance protects the government, payment protects the subs. Payment bond notices, thirty days from first furnishing, ninety days from last. No liens on public property, ever.

That is the whole domain. Eleven questions, and every number they can ask you was in there. The five you have to own cold are twenty, thirty, ninety, fifteen, and one year. Run the drill track until those roll off without thinking, and this becomes the easiest eleven points on the exam.
